title: About Malaria

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Malaria is not endemic in the United States. This means it does not regularly occur or spread in the U.S. In a typical year, the U.S. reports about 2,000 cases of malaria. Most of these cases are in people who contract malaria while traveling to another country where malaria spreads and return to the U.S. On rare occasions, local transmission (spread) occurs because of an imported case of malaria. People do not spread malaria to other people, like the common cold or the flu. Also, malaria is not sexually transmitted.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Malaria symptoms range from very mild illness to severe disease and even death. Early symptoms can include:

sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Headache, muscle aches, and tiredness

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea may also occur

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: If not treated quickly, the infection can become severe.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Severe symptoms can include

sections.heading: Symptoms

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Seizures

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Mental confusion

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Coma

sections.heading: Causes and Risk
sections.text: Malaria is a disease caused by a parasite. Anopheles mosquitoes are the type of mosquito that transmit malaria from one person to another. Not all Anopheles mosquitoes have malaria, but if they bite a person with malaria, they can become infectious. Once they bite another person, this continues the cycle of spreading malaria from mosquito to people.

sections.text: See a healthcare provider as soon as possible if

sections.heading: Testing and diagnosis
sections.text: You are experiencing any of the symptoms of malaria, and

sections.heading: Testing and diagnosis
sections.text: You have traveled in the last year to or from an area where malaria occurs.

sections.heading: Testing and diagnosis
sections.text: Only a healthcare provider can diagnose malaria. A lab test will confirm malaria using a small sample of your blood.

sections.text: Prescription drugs can treat and cure malaria. The types of drugs and length of treatment depends on

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: The type of malaria,

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: Where (geographic location) the person was infected, and

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: How sick they are when treatment starts.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text: Other important factors are age and whether the patient is pregnant.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: If traveling to an area where malaria spreads, talk with your healthcare provider about medications you can take to prevent malaria.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Avoid areas with high mosquito activity, especially during late evening and at night. This is when Anopheles mosquitoes that spread malaria bite.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Use a bug spray approved by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants and socks.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Keep windows and doors closed or covered with screens to keep mosquitoes out of your house.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Repair broken screens on windows, doors, porches, and patios.
